WalkthroughText: A constructor is special method-like code that runs when you create an object with the "new" keyword, and its job is to set up the instance variables stored inside that object on the heap. A default constructor takes no parameters and usually assigns fixed starting values (or Java auto-generates one that leaves fields at 0/null/false if you write no constructors yourself). A parameterized constructor takes arguments so the caller can supply custom starting values instead of relying on defaults. Watching the stack frame and heap object side by side shows exactly how the constructor's parameters (on the stack) get copied into the object's fields (on the heap) during construction.

Choices: title = "Untitled", pages must be given explicitly or a compile error occurs
A compile error occurs because Book has two constructors
PracticeItems.Explanation: Book() has no arguments, so Java matches the no-argument (default) constructor, which explicitly sets title to "Untitled" and pages to 0. It is legal in Java to overload constructors, so having two constructors does not cause an error. The second constructor is simply not called here because no arguments were passed.

Choices: It compiles and creates a Point with x = 0 and y = 0
It compiles and creates a Point with x and y uninitialized (garbage values)
It does not compile because there is no no-argument constructor available
It compiles because Java automatically creates a no-argument constructor even when other constructors exist
PracticeItems.Explanation: Java only auto-generates a no-argument default constructor if the class defines NO constructors at all. Since Point defines a parameterized constructor, Java does not add a no-arg one, so calling new Point() with no arguments fails to compile because there's no matching constructor signature.

Choices: A compile error occurs because this(...) cannot be used in a constructor
color = "Black", speed = 0, but only after both constructors' bodies run redundantly
PracticeItems.Explanation: The no-arg constructor uses this("Black", 0) to delegate to the two-argument constructor, which sets color to "Black" and speed to 0. This is a valid and common technique to avoid duplicating initialization code between overloaded constructors. It does not cause a compile error, and the no-arg constructor's own body doesn't run separately afterward since this(...) call replaces that initialization step (there is no other code in the no-arg constructor).

WalkthroughSteps.Caption: We start in main, which is about to create two Dog objects — one with the default constructor and one with a parameterized constructor.
First, main calls 'new Dog()' with no arguments, so a new Dog constructor frame is pushed onto the stack.
Java allocates a new Dog object on the heap with default placeholder fields before the constructor body runs.
Inside the no-argument constructor, the body explicitly sets name to "Rex" and age to 1, since there are no parameters to use.
The default constructor finishes, so its frame is popped off the stack, and main's variable d1 now refers to this new Dog object.
Next, main calls 'new Dog("Buddy", 3)', passing arguments, so a new constructor frame is pushed with parameters n and a stored in memory.
A second Dog object is allocated on the heap, again starting with default placeholder field values.
This time the constructor body copies the parameter values from the stack frame into the object's fields: name = n and age = a.
The parameterized constructor finishes and its frame pops off the stack, leaving main's variable d2 pointing at this custom-built Dog.

Now we have two Dog objects on the heap: d1 built with fixed default values ("Rex", 1), and d2 built with caller-supplied values ("Buddy", 3) — the core difference between default and parameterized constructors.
